prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned prose, grounded in poetry, that builds memory, the body and dream into an expansive metaphysical project.

statement.case_for: My laureate is unchanged: Cărtărescu, B042. The exchange did not give me new evidence about the works, so I have not changed my judgment of them. It did change how I state the conditions on that judgment. On public knowledge, which I have not independently verified, the case rests on voice and architecture together. The Blinding trilogy and Solenoid use memory, the body and dream as the structural principle of very large books, not as imagery laid over a conventional plot. In these works formal ambition and imaginative depth appear to be one thing. The project reads as cumulative: a poetic foundation, then large prose cycles that extend one vision. That bears on sustained quality across an oeuvre and not on a single breakthrough. On the chair's question about citation scope, I would centre the citation on the prose cycles and name the poetry only as the formative ground. Carlberg and Sem-Sandberg named prose and poetry together in round 1, but their statements also say the prose should carry the claim. My own knowledge of the poetry in translation is the weakest part of my assessment, so I do not want the citation to claim more than I can support. I do not think this choice changes any supporter's position, but it is the honest scope. I weigh the case on the common criteria and not on how many colleagues share a first choice. The chair notes that four supporters coincide with the four-vote threshold, and I give that no weight as merit.
statement.case_against: My reservations are the ones I recorded in round 1, and the chair's questions sharpen them without answering them. I am judging dense, long-breathed Romanian prose through translation, and the qualities I value most (rhythm, syntactic patterning, wordplay) are the ones most exposed to loss. I cannot show from the evidence supplied that the very long late books earn their length throughout. I argued that the case survives some unevenness because it rests on the trilogy and Solenoid. That is a conditional defence and not a demonstration, and Olsson's fourth-place ranking is a serious expression of the same worry. Coverage of the poetry and early work is thin, so the whole-oeuvre claim rests disproportionately on the late novels. Carson's formal invention is more directly legible to the committee in English, and Adonis's remaking of a poetic language is the clearest transformation of a language on the list. If the committee had credible readings from Romanian-language readers saying that the late novels repeat a method instead of deepening it, I would move to Carson as my first alternative. If instead the poetry and early prose proved weak, I would require the citation to rest entirely on the prose. I would need to ask whether that narrower claim still counts as a whole oeuvre.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Adonis first for a decades-long remaking of Arabic poetic language and ranks Cărtărescu fourth because he cannot tell whether the very long late volumes hold up evenly. He asks that the committee test whether the late novels are consolidation or accumulation, and he keeps the citation on the poetry and not on the essays or public role.
responses.response: I agree with the citation discipline you propose for Adonis, and I hold myself to the same standard for Cărtărescu: the work carries the claim and nothing else. On evenness, I can only say what I look for. In a consolidating project, later volumes should change the problem they inherit, with the architecture altering how earlier images read. In an accumulating one, they should repeat the method at greater length. From public knowledge I read the trilogy and Solenoid as the first kind, but I cannot verify it, and you are right to treat that as the open test. I also take your parity point seriously. Prose built on large-scale structure is probably somewhat less exposed to translation loss than prosodic verse, but I would not count that as an advantage over Adonis, and I do not want it to count against him either. If the committee can obtain Arabic-language and Romanian-language readings, I would put the same questions to both: do the later works change the project or repeat it, and what does translation lose that a reader in the original would not forgive?

responses.point: Sward ranks Carson first for a voice recognizable across genres and a sustained reconfiguration of genre. She answers the signal-books worry by pointing to continuity of concerns (grief, desire, the fragment, the afterlife of ancient texts) from the early essays to the late book-objects. She argues that the English text is directly legible to the committee, and she accepts that linguistic achievement through dialogue with source texts is harder to measure.
responses.response: Your answer on continuity is the best reply to the signal-books objection, and it moves me. I now think the question is less whether Carson's work is sustained than whether a citation can name what is sustained without leaning on book design or on translation. Your proposal to centre the citation on the lyric and essayistic writing is a real answer to that. I accept that a fragment made to speak in a new register is linguistic work, and I withdraw any suggestion that the dialogue with source texts makes the achievement derivative. My remaining difference is where I place the weight. In Cărtărescu the architecture is carried by the text itself, whereas some of Carson's most celebrated effects depend on the physical form of the book. That is a difference of kind, not a ranking of standing, and I could be persuaded otherwise by evidence that her text-only work holds the same depth. I also grant your legibility point, which is the strongest practical argument for Carson. It counts against my own reliance on translation, and it is why she stays my first alternative.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first and says he would move toward Carson or Adonis if the evidence beyond the best-known volumes proved thin. He treats the unevenness caution as a live condition and not a formality, and he asks whether density becomes mere pattern.
responses.response: I share your condition and would state it the same way. My case rests on the trilogy and Solenoid, so if the committee finds the evidence outside those books thin, the right response is to narrow the citation to the prose and to say plainly that it was reached through translation, not to claim more. I would also put your question about density as pattern to my own reading. The test I use is whether the patterning does work in the book, for example by changing how earlier passages read or by carrying the book's argument about memory and the body. From public knowledge I think it does, but that is a judgment, not a verification. Where I would go further than you is on what would change my vote. If Romanian-language readers judged the late books repetitive, I would move to Carson. Thin evidence on the poetry alone would not move me, because I would simply leave the poetry out of the citation.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first for voice and imaginative scale. She proposes testing whether Solenoid and the Blinding trilogy each earn their length through structure or let scale substitute for it. She asks that any citation say the claim concerns the prose project and not the full poetic corpus. She also questions whether Carson's work is sustained depth or formal experiment.
responses.response: Your test is the right one and I accept it, including your request that the citation be explicit about scope. That is the reason I now centre the wording on the prose cycles and mention poetry only as ground. On your remarks about my own ballot: I ranked Wright fourth, and my round-1 file did not argue her case. Your point about the small number of major novels and the question of whether English carries the oral registers is fair, and I do not have a developed oeuvre-level answer to it. It is a reason she sits below the three leading candidates for me, not a reason to dismiss her. On Carson, your question about sustained depth versus formal experiment is the same one I put to my own first choice, and Sward's continuity argument has moved me a little on it. I would keep us from treating the two questions as symmetrical, though. For Cărtărescu the doubt is evenness across very long books. For Carson it is how much of the achievement a text-only citation can name.

uncertainties: How much of the density, rhythm and wordplay of Cărtărescu's Romanian prose survives in translation, and whether the committee's reading reflects the original.

Whether the very long late novels are evenly sustained or sometimes repeat a method. I cannot settle this from the supplied descriptions or from public knowledge, and I have read nothing here that resolves it.
How the poetry and early fiction compare with the late novels. My coverage is limited, which is why I would scope the citation to the prose.

Whether Romanian-language or Arabic-language readings could be obtained, and whether they would be independent enough to settle the evenness questions. I assume nothing about their existence or content.

How the formal achievement of Carson (hybrid and book-object forms, English legible directly) and Adonis (Arabic prosody, judged through translation) should be weighed against a prose-architecture case when each is mediated differently.
Whether the later poetry of Adonis holds the level of the major earlier collections, which neither I nor the supplied evidence can establish.

I have not independently verified any source and rely on public knowledge and the shortlist descriptions. I do not regard the evidence as so insufficient that I would put P000 ahead of the leading candidates, but the stated conditions remain.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. It records no personal, professional or collaborative connection to any shortlisted writer. My own literary practice (parallel narrative structures, myth and fairy-tale registers, and a biography of Selma Lagerlöf) is context only and is not evidence that I favour any candidate. No disclosure has changed since round 1. This is a disclosure and is not adjudicated here.
